TITLE: Evaluating Baseline Methods for Frame Selection in Long-Video Question Answering
PROPOSAL: We will experimentally evaluate the state-of-the-art VLM-based approach (analyzing query-frame pairs) and a query-related frame selection method (using a lightweight model for similarity) on the TVQA and Ego4D benchmarks, with the goal of understanding their performance on these challenging tasks. We will compare their question-answering accuracy and computational cost, focusing on frame selection's impact on reducing the VLM's computational overhead.
CONTROLS: Uniform frame sampling (fixed interval), and a random frame sampling baseline to represent simple methods.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (24 hours using 4 8GB GPU machines).
PREDICTION: The VLM-based approach will outperform the lightweight similarity-based method on question-answering accuracy, but incur a high computational cost. The uniform frame sampling baseline will serve as a useful comparison for frame selection's impact.

Considering the research question, this first experiment helps to understand the gap between current approaches and the goal of concise yet comprehensive frame selection. By comparing baseline methods, we set the stage for developing more efficient strategies that best/approximate the results of the VLM-based approach while controlling the computational cost.

TITLE: Query-Aware Frame Selection via Multi-Task Learning
PROPOSAL: To better represent queries and frames, we design a multi-task learning framework that trains a single VLM on both query-frame similarity and frame classification tasks. We fine-tune a CLIP-style model on these tasks in a joint manner, using the TVQA and Ego4D datasets. This approach aims to leverage the benefits of lightweight similarity models (efficient computation) while improving their relevance estimates for complex queries.
CONTROLS: Our proposed method as well as a variant without the classification task, and CLIP as an ablation study to verify the value of multi-task learning.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (40 hours using 4 8GB GPU machines or 8 hours using 16 8GB GPU machines).
PREDICTION: We expect this approach to yield a better question-answering accuracy and a reasonable trade-off between accuracy and computational cost, but its performance might degrade on simple queries where the lightweight similarity model already performs well.

TITLE: Hierarchical Video Frame Sampling
PROPOSAL: Inspired by the success of hierarchical models in sequence prediction, we propose a hierarchical framework for frame selection. This framework samples frames at two levels: a high-level selector chooses promising frames based on a query-relevant index, followed by a low-level selector that refines the selection using a differentiable sampling strategy. The high-level selector reduces the dimensionality of the video and enables efficient initial frame selection, while the low-level selector generates a diverse and compact set of frames from the high-level selector's output. We train a variant of the query-aware multi-task learning framework for both selectors, aiming to leverage their strengths in capturing both local and global video information.

TITLE: Online Adaptation of Frame Sampling for Dynamic Videos
PROPOSAL: Current frame sampling methods focus on offline frameworks that cannot adapt to changing query complexities or dynamically adapting video contexts. To address this limitation, we propose an online adaptive sampling strategy that updates the sampling weights in real-time as the video and query are processed. We leverage recent advancements in online learning and adaptive methods to learn a dynamic sampling policy that can adjust to changes in the video and query conditions. Our model is trained to minimize an online loss function that balances the accuracy of the VLM and the efficiency of the sampling strategy.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Efficient VLM-based Frame Selection for Long-Video Question Answering
PROPOSAL: We propose a new approach called VITESSE (Video Inference-driven Stratified Chunk Extraction) that efficiently selects a concise yet comprehensive set of frames for long-video question answering using VLMs. In VITESSE, we first use a lightweight similarity model to identify the most relevant segments of the video, and then use a VLM to analyze these segments in a hierarchical manner, selecting a subset of frames in each segment. This approach reduces the computational cost of exhaustive VLM-based analysis while retaining its effectiveness.
CONTROLS: We compare VITESSE with existing frame selection methods, such as uniform sampling and query-related frame selection using lightweight multi-modal models. We also ablate the effect of different segmenting strategies and VLM architectures.
COST: 500 GPU hours (due to smaller computational cost compared to exhaustive VLM-based analysis).
PREDICTION: VITESSE will demonstrate significant improvements in question-answering accuracy compared to existing frame selection methods, with a reduction in computational cost of at least 50%. VITESSE may fail for very long videos or those with complex query requirements, which may require more sophisticated analysis. 

Note: I used the GPU-hours as an estimate, but the actual number of GPU-hours might vary depending on the specific setup and dataset used. 

Domains: This proposal is relevant to the experimental domains of long-video question answering and egocentric video question answering.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Hierarchical Video Inference with Attention-Guided Segmentation
PROPOSAL: We propose to augment VITESSE (from proposal 1) with an attention-guided segmentation mechanism to improve the selection of frames within each segment. In this mechanism, we use a VLM to analyze the frames within a segment and output an attention map that highlights the query-relevant moments. We then segment the frames within each segment based on this attention map to select the most relevant frames. This approach refines the selection process by adaptively focusing on the most critical parts of the segment.
CONTROLS: We compare the attention-guided segmentation mechanism with traditional fixed-size segmentation strategies (e.g., segmenting every 16 frames). We also ablate the effect of different VLM architectures and attention mechanisms.
COST: 200 GPU hours (due to the additional computational cost of attention-guided segmentation).
PREDICTION: The attention-guided segmentation mechanism will improve the question-answering accuracy of VITESSE by at least 15% compared to traditional fixed-size segmentation strategies. However, it may require a larger batch size or more sophisticated hardware acceleration to handle the increased computational cost.

Domains: This proposal is relevant to the experimental domains of long-video question answering, egocentric video question answering, and temporal video grounding.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: VideoQA Refinement using Localized Self-Attention Modules
PROPOSAL: We propose to incorporate localized self-attention modules within the VLM architecture used in VITESSE (from proposal 1) to focus on query-relevant parts of the video. These modules employ spatial attention to graphically extract and exploit spatiotemporal dependencies between frames within a segment, mitigating information loss and providing a more fine-grained representation of the information. This approach complements VITESSE by capturing more nuanced and detailed relationships between frames.
CONTROLS: We compare the localized self-attention modules with vanilla VLM architectures and ablate the effect of different attention mechanisms and module sizes. We also evaluate the sensitivity of the results to the trade-off between computational cost and refined representation accuracy.
COST: 150 GPU hours (due to the additional computational cost of localized self-attention).
PREDICTION: The localized self-attention modules will lead to an improvement in question-answering accuracy of VITESSE by at least 20% compared to vanilla VLM architectures, likely due to their ability to identify finer-grained frame relationships. However, overfitting to spatiotemporal patterns might occur for small datasets, and computational cost could become a limiting factor for larger videos.

Domains: This proposal is relevant to the experimental domains of long-video question answering, egocentric video question answering, and temporal video grounding.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: VideoQA Refinement using Global and Localized Self-Attention Modules
PROPOSAL: We propose to modify the localized self-attention modules (from revised proposal 3) to work in a hierarchical manner, coupled with a new layer of VLM that incorporates global self-attention to capture high-level semantic relationships throughout the whole video. The global self-attention layer combines segment-level representations to produce a dense, contextualized video embedding. The localized self-attention modules are used to further refine this representation by focusing on query-relevant parts of the video.
CONTROLS: We compare the combination of global and localized self-attention modules with other attention mechanisms, such as vanilla VLM and dynamic convolution. We also ablate the effect of the hierarchical attention architecture and module sizes.
COST: 250 GPU hours (due to the increased computational cost of global self-attention and hierarchical architecture).
PREDICTION: The global and localized self-attention modules will demonstrate a substantial improvement in question-answering accuracy over vanilla VLM architectures and separated global/local attention, likely due to their ability to identify both fine-grained frame relationships and higher-level semantic connections.

Domains: This proposal remains relevant to the experimental domains of long-video question answering, egocentric video question answering, and temporal video grounding.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Curriculum Learning for VLM-based Video Frame Selection
PROPOSAL: We propose a curriculum learning approach to progressively improve the performance of VLM-based video frame selection. The approach involves creating a hierarchical curriculum where the model is first trained on a series of simplified tasks (e.g., binary classification, segment-level question answering) before progressing to more complex ones (e.g., long-video question answering). By leveraging prior knowledge and avoiding overfitting, the model adapts more efficiently to the high-dimensional video space.
CONTROLS: We compare the curriculum learning approach with a standard one-shot learning strategy, where the VLM is fine-tuned directly from a pre-trained state. We also ablate the effect of different curriculum learning strategies, such as hand-crafted milestones and automated difficulty progression.
COST: 100 GPU hours (due to the incremental training process).
PREDICTION: Curriculum learning will lead to an improvement in question-answering accuracy by at least 10% compared to standard one-shot learning, likely due to the gradual buildup of knowledge and avoidance of overfitting. However, it may require a more complex setup and careful configuration of milestones.

Domains: This proposal remains relevant to the experimental domains of long-video question answering, egocentric video question answering, and temporal video grounding.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Temporal Knowledge Transfer for VLM-based Video Frame Selection
PROPOSAL: We propose a temporal knowledge transfer mechanism to leverage external video databases and question-answering repositories to pre-train a VLM-based video frame selection model. This approach involves fine-tuning the VLM on these external datasets to learn generalizable temporal features and transfer knowledge across different domains and tasks. We then adapt this pre-trained model to the target long-video question answering task.
CONTROLS: We compare the temporal knowledge transfer approach with standard fine-tuning on the target task alone, as well as with a meta-learning strategy that adapts to the target task in an incremental manner. We also evaluate the sensitivity of the results to the size and diversity of the external datasets.
COST: 300 GPU hours (due to the pre-training process on large-scale external datasets).
PREDICTION: Temporal knowledge transfer will demonstrate a significant improvement in question-answering accuracy compared to standard fine-tuning, likely due to the ability to learn generalizable temporal features and adapt to new tasks. However, it may require access to large-scale external datasets and careful selection of relevant knowledge.

Domains: This proposal remains relevant to the experimental domains of long-video question answering, egocentric video question answering, and temporal video grounding.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Uncertainty-based Active Learning for Efficient Video Frame Selection
PROPOSAL: We propose an uncertainty-based active learning approach to select the most informative frames from a long video for VLM-based question answering. We use Bayesian neural networks to predict the uncertainty of VLM's predictions for each frame and select the frames with highest uncertainty. These frames are then used to augment the training data and adapt the VLM's parameters.
CONTROLS: We compare the uncertainty-based active learning approach with a random selection method, as well as a fixed-size sampling strategy. We also evaluate the sensitivity of the results to the uncertainty metrics used and the adaptation rate of the VLM's parameters.
COST: 80 GPU hours (due to the iterative active learning process).
PREDICTION: Uncertainty-based active learning will lead to an improvement in question-answering accuracy by at least 8% compared to random selection and fixed-size sampling, likely due to the selection of the most informative frames. However, it may require a careful balance between exploration and exploitation.

Domains: This proposal remains relevant to the experimental domains of long-video question answering, egocentric video question answering, and temporal video grounding.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Multi-Task Learning for Video Question Answering and Vid2Text
PROPOSAL: We propose a multi-task learning approach to leverage the similarities between video question answering and video-to-text (Vid2Text) tasks. We jointly train a VLM on both tasks, sharing the weights between them. This allows the VLM to learn a more robust and generalizable representation of video content and its relationships with text queries. We also incorporate a curriculum learning schedule to adapt the VLM to the target tasks.
CONTROLS: We compare the multi-task learning approach with single-task training on each task separately. We also evaluate the sensitivity of the results to the number of shared layers and the curriculum learning schedule.
COST: 400 GPU hours (due to the joint training process on both tasks).
PREDICTION: Multi-task learning will demonstrate an improvement in question-answering accuracy of at least 12% compared to single-task training, likely due to the robust and generalizable representation learned by the VLM. However, it may require careful balancing of the tasks and their respective losses.

Domains: This proposal is particularly relevant to the experimental domains of long-video question answering, vid2text, and egocentric video question answering.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: Video-Aware Data Augmentation for Video Question Answering
PROPOSAL: We propose a video-aware data augmentation approach to generate synthetic video clips by interpolating or perturbing the original frames. We design a VLM-based generator that adapts to the specific use case of video question answering and incorporates various video-specific transformations, such as frame temporal interpolation and spatial distortion. The generated synthetic clips are then used to augment the training data.
CONTROLS: We compare the video-aware data augmentation approach with traditional image-level data augmentation and evaluate the sensitivity of the results to the type and frequency of augmentations applied.
COST: 120 GPU hours (due to the generation of synthetic clips).
PREDICTION: Video-aware data augmentation will demonstrate an improvement in question-answering accuracy of at least 9% compared to traditional image-level augmentation, likely due to the ability to effectively create realistic and informative synthetic clips. However, it may require careful calibration of the augmentation pipeline.

Domains: This proposal remains relevant to the experimental domains of long-video question answering, egocentric video question answering, and temporal video grounding.

ACTION: ADD 9
TITLE: Real-world Evaluation of Human-in-the-Loop for VideoQA
PROPOSAL: We propose a human-in-the-loop (HITL) approach to evaluate and refine the proposed video question answering models on real-world data. We design a human labeling protocol to collect high-quality labels for a diverse set of video question answering tasks and use these labels to evaluate the performance of our proposed models. We also design a refinement protocol to collect more labels for challenging samples and use these additional labels to adapt and improve our models.
CONTROLS: We compare the HITL approach with traditional evaluation metrics (e.g., accuracy, F1 score) and evaluate the sensitivity of the results to the labeling protocol and refinement process.
COST: 500 manual hours (due to the human labeling and refinement process).
PREDICTION: The HITL approach will demonstrate an improvement in question-answering accuracy of at least 15% compared to traditional evaluation metrics, likely due to the ability to effectively capture nuanced aspects of human understanding. However, it may require careful design and implementation of the human labeling and refinement protocols.

Domains: This proposal is particularly relevant to the experimental domains of real-world video question answering and remains investigable with the experimental dataset DCASE-2020 (as not evaluated within our LL time).

This concludes our list of proposals to address the research question of efficient video frame selection for long-video question answering using VLMs.

We will use the DiDeMo (Dense Event Description from Multimedia) dataset, which consists of 6,846 video-grounding questions, and evaluate our approach on the standard Temporal Grounding Benchmark (TGB) metrics.

title: progressive ranking with sequentially-abstracting transformers
PROPOSAL: Investigate a novel ranking mechanism using a sequentially-abstracting transformer (SeT) that generates progressively abstract representations of query and video features. These abstract features are ranked to select the most relevant frames, and the top-ranked frames are then used by a strong VLM to answer queries. We will train and evaluate our system on the ActivityNet-QA dataset, and evaluate its performance using mean rank, mean recall, and accuracy at the top-K retrieved frames.
CONTROLS: Compare against a ranking mechanism that uniformly samples frames from the entire video and a strong VLM applied to the entire video.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our method will improve the accuracy of the strong VLM by 8-12% over the controls, as it captures the key aspects of the query using its sequentially-abstracting mechanism.

Note: hypothesize that sequentially-abstracting transformers maintain some of the key properties of traditional transformers, such as the ability to model long-range dependencies and interact with query features at multiple levels of abstraction.
